entries.place: Definition of the positive norm subgroup (45.1)
entries.reason: If no real prime is ramified, the printed positivity condition is vacuous and admits zero. The reduced norm of a unit is nonzero.
entries.verified_by: The definition and the immediately following norm-image formula (45.2), together with the identical nonzero convention in Volume I (7.47) and (51.22).

entries.place: Proof of the local maximal-order theorem (45.13), conjugation and epsilon
entries.original: $pi_D^(-1) omega pi_D$ and $omega pi_D^(-1) omega^(-1) pi_D$
entries.corrected: $pi_D omega pi_D^(-1)$ and $omega pi_D omega^(-1) pi_D^(-1)$

entries.place: Theorem (45.18), Step 2, the ideal following the homology sequence
entries.reason: The following computation uses the generators $overline(x)-1$ of the augmentation ideal.
entries.verified_by: The displayed action $(overline(x)-1)n=[x,n]$ in the same proof.

entries.original: Every noncentral normal subgroup of an open subgroup of $SL_n lr((A))$ is open, for semisimple $A$.
entries.corrected: Apply Borel’s theorem separately in each simple component of $A$. Each intersection with the kernel contains a noncentral elementary matrix; their product is open.
entries.reason: For a product algebra, $SL_2 lr((R)) times lr({1})$ is noncentral and normal in $SL_2 lr((R)) times SL_2 lr((R))$, but is not open. The actual kernel meets every simple factor in a suitable noncentral subgroup.
entries.verified_by: Componentwise normality and elementary matrices with coefficients $c e_i in Lambda$, followed by the simple-factor theorem. Wall (1973), Theorem9, and Bhandari–Sehgal (1991), Theorem2.1, supply the stated characteristic-zero scope.

entries.place: Theorem (45.31), matrix-ring setup and residue commutators
entries.reason: $GL_2 lr((bb(F)_2))$ has order 6 and commutator subgroup of order 3, although $K_1 lr((bb(F)_2))=1$. Size 3 makes each residue matrix factor have size at least 3, so its determinant kernel equals its commutator subgroup.
entries.verified_by: Elementary generation of the special linear group and the commutator relation with a third index. Exact finite computations confirm the size-two exception and the size-three example.

entries.place: Theorem (45.31), closedness of the Whitehead kernel
entries.original: The kernel is closed by Corollary (45.23).
entries.corrected: Use adic continuity of $K_1$. The kernel is the intersection of the kernels of the finite reduction maps to $K_1 lr((Lambda slash pi^m Lambda))$, and is therefore closed.
entries.reason: Corollary (45.23) inherits characteristic-zero hypotheses. Adic continuity applies because the ring is complete for powers of $pi Lambda$ and the quotients are finite of prime-power order; it also covers equal characteristic.
entries.verified_by: de Frutos-Fernández, Macías Castillo and Martínez Marqués (2026), Definition 4.1 and Proposition 4.4, Compositio Mathematica 162, 873–875, DOI 10.1017/S0010437X26103108. The published extension proof invokes Fukaya–Kato for its radical case.

entries.original: The reduced norm carries $K_1^F lr((R G))$ into the center of $R G$.
entries.corrected: The reduced norm carries $K_1^F lr((R G))$ into the center of $F G$.
entries.reason: The central reduced norm need not have integral group-ring coefficients.
entries.verified_by: The reduced-norm construction in (46.10). For the rotation r of D₈ over R=Z₂[i], its central reduced norm is (1+r+r³−r²)/2, which is not in RG.

entries.place: Theorem (46.10), Step 5, definition of the image of 1−σ
entries.reason: The inverse belongs to the value σ(h), not to the automorphism σ.
entries.verified_by: The commutator calculation in (46.10), Step 5. For H=C₃² with a nonidentity unipotent automorphism σ of order 3 and a fixed element h of order 3, the corrected value is 1 while the printed value is h²≠1. This satisfies the nonabelian semidirect-product case.

entries.place: Lemma (46.18), restriction on a coset basis
entries.original: A permutation matrix whose determinant is the sign times the transfer.
entries.corrected: A monomial matrix whose permutation and diagonal factors give the sign times the transfer in $K_1 lr((R H))$.
entries.reason: The nonzero matrix entries are elements of H, and RH need not be commutative.
entries.verified_by: The left-coset basis and the transfer formula in Volume I (13.11). Factoring the monomial matrix is a valid K₁ calculation without a noncommutative determinant.

entries.place: Lemma (46.18), tensor-action identity and scope of its proof
entries.original: $[X] [R G,g_l] = g^(rank_R X)$; the proof concludes both assertions without qualification.
entries.corrected: $[X] [R G,g_l] = eta_* [rho_X lr((g^(-1)))] dot g^d$, where $d=rank_R X$. Retain the first assertion with an explicit qualification that its tensor-stability step requires the finite-order matrix class to equal its determinant; the given argument does not establish this for arbitrary P.I.D. Write the second group as a product of subgroups, with scalar intersection $eta_* S K_1 lr((R))$. Prove (46.19) separately using integer lattices.
entries.reason: Untwisting contributes the full scalar K₁(R) class. Even over Z the sign lattice of C₂ gives −g rather than g. No universal determinant simplification is established by this argument.
entries.verified_by: The right-module isomorphism x⊗h↦xh⁻¹⊗h conjugates the action to x⊗h↦xg⁻¹⊗gh. Augmentation identifies the exact missing condition and splits the scalar inclusion; its intersection with SK₁(RG) is the scalar SK₁(R). For (46.19), the action matrix is over Z and K₁(Z)={±1}. The retained first assertion is neither refuted nor declared a general open theorem here.

entries.original: is p-torsionfree if and only if every indicated hyperelementary subgroup has p-torsionfree Whitehead group
entries.corrected: is p-torsionfree if every indicated hyperelementary subgroup has p-torsionfree Whitehead group
entries.reason: The localized Frobenius argument proves sufficiency; necessity for Wh is false under the stated hypotheses.
entries.verified_by: Oliver (1988), Theorem 14.1 and introduction Example 6(i): Wh(S₉)=0, but H=C₃³≤S₉ has SK₁(ZH)=C₃³. Proposition (46.1) makes its intersection with ±H trivial, so it injects into Wh(H). The sufficient implication for both Wh and Wh^F follows from (46.21)(ii).

entries.original: $delta_1 Lambda delta_1 = (S delta_1) compose P = (S delta_1) compose P_1$
entries.reason: Only homogeneous terms whose group element stabilizes δ₁ survive the corner.
entries.verified_by: The definition of P₁ and the orthogonality of the primitive idempotents in (46.24), Step 3: δ₁(sx)δ₁=0 unless x fixes δ₁.

entries.original: The matrix-ring description is asserted for the stated transitive p-adic action without an unramified hypothesis.
entries.corrected: Require that $F_1$ be unramified over its fixed field $F_1^(P_1 slash P_0)$, retaining that requirement in the extension to abelian $P_0$.
entries.reason: The preceding proof uses the identification of the quotient action with the residue Galois group; it need not hold in the ramified case.
entries.verified_by: Theorem (46.24), Step 4. The skew ring Z₂[i]∘C₂, with conjugation action, has a unital quotient F₂. The claimed matrix description would force M₂(Z₂), which admits no such quotient. The actual preceding application to RC is already unramified.

entries.original: $op("Wh")^QQ lr((ZZ G)) tilde.equiv C^+ slash "torsion subgroup of" C^+$
entries.corrected: $op("Wh")^QQ lr((ZZ G)) tilde.equiv U slash "torsion subgroup of" U$, where $U=op("nr") K_1 lr((ZZ G)) subset.eq C^+$.
entries.reason: The norm image of the integral group ring, rather than the whole ambient field-unit group, is required.
entries.verified_by: Theorem (46.4) identifies the torsion of the integral norm image with the norm of ±G. For G=1 the Whitehead group is zero, while Q×/{±1} is not.

entries.original: $bold(M) lr((g^(-1))) = bold(P) overline(bold(M)(g)) bold(P)^(-1)$ and the subsequent complex-conjugate similarity claim
entries.corrected: $bold(M) lr((g^(-1))) = bold(P) overline(bold(M)(g))^t bold(P)^(-1)$; transpose the outer matrix indices as well, giving conjugate-transpose similarity.
entries.reason: Group inversion is an anti-involution, so a transpose is necessary in both matrix layers.
entries.verified_by: An averaged invariant Hermitian form gives M(g⁻¹)=H⁻¹ overline(M(g))ᵗH. Taking determinants gives precisely the conjugation of reduced norms required in the hint.

entries.original: The logarithmic map on all $F_j^dot$ has a free lattice image of rank $m-1$ and torsion kernel.
entries.corrected: Apply the logarithmic map to the algebraic-integer units of $F_j$. Its kernel is the roots of unity; omit the unused rank assertion and apply it to $overline(alpha) slash alpha$.
entries.reason: The asserted field-unit lattice already fails for $F_j=QQ$. The actual reduced norms of integral invertible matrices are algebraic units.
entries.verified_by: Both u and u⁻¹ preserve an integral representation lattice. Character fields lie in a cyclotomic field, so all embeddings commute with conjugation; every conjugate of overline(α)/α has absolute value 1. The root-of-unity conclusion proves the original exercise.

entries.reason: A p-adic ring may contain p-power roots of unity that disappear in the residue field.
entries.verified_by: The Teichmüller splitting in Exercise 45.11. For R=Z₃[ζ₃], the residue unit group has order 2 but R× contains ζ₃ of order 3; reduction and Teichmüller lifting identify exactly the prime-to-p torsion.

entries.reason: The product must include both the 2-adic and real places.
entries.verified_by: The preceding factorization (47.46) proves the full-place product. For a=b=3 the product over odd primes alone is −1, since the factor at 3 is −1 and all other odd factors are 1.

entries.reason: The exercise covers all finite fields, including $F_(2^r)$ for $r>1$.
entries.verified_by: For even q the unit group is cyclic of odd order q−1. If x generates it, the diagonal symbol {x,x} has order dividing both 2, by antisymmetry, and q−1, by bimultiplicativity, hence is trivial.

entries.place: Theorem (48.4), reference to the earlier induction argument
entries.reason: The induction argument occurs before (48.3).
entries.verified_by: The displayed Artin-exponent induction calculation immediately preceding Theorem (48.3).

entries.original: For each $p$, the Sylow $p$-subgroup has the form $C_p times C_(p^n)$.
entries.corrected: For each $p$ for which $G_p$ is noncyclic, the Sylow $p$-subgroup has the form $C_p times C_(p^n)$.
entries.reason: The original global alternatives omit groups with cyclic Sylow subgroups at some primes and the indicated rank-two form at others.
entries.verified_by: Oliver (1988), Theorem 14.2(iii) and its proof: each Sylow subgroup may be cyclic or C_p×C_(p^n), unless the whole group is elementary abelian 2. For example C₂×C₃² has trivial SK₁ but satisfies none of the literal original alternatives.

entries.corrected: $G_p$ is one of $1$, $C_p$, $C_(p^2)$, or $C_p times C_p$.
entries.reason: The hypothesis $abs(G_p)<=p^2$ also allows orders $1$ and $p$.
entries.verified_by: Classification of groups of order at most p² and the corrected Theorem (48.6). The added cases have cyclic p-elementary subgroups and do not require narrowing the theorem.

entries.place: Reference to the Jacobinski Cancellation Theorem
entries.original: In §51A we prove the fundamental Jacobinski Cancellation Theorem
entries.corrected: In §51C we prove the fundamental Jacobinski Cancellation Theorem
entries.reason: The cancellation theorem is in §51C; §51A treats the Eichler condition.
entries.verified_by: The actual headings of §§51A and 51C and Theorem (51.24).

entries.original: $gamma: S K_0 lr((Lambda)) -> product.co_P S K_1 lr((Lambda_P))$
entries.corrected: $gamma: S K_0 lr((Lambda)) -> product.co_P S K_0 lr((Lambda_P))$
entries.reason: The map is induced by extension of scalars on K₀.

entries.place: Theorem (49.40), proof, projection onto the exceptional primes
entries.original: There is an embedding $i: frak(O)^+ -> product_(P in S) frak(O)_P^dot$; identify $frak(O)^+$ with $i(frak(O)^+)$.
entries.corrected: There is a natural homomorphism $i: frak(O)^+ -> product_(P in S) frak(O)_P^dot$; $frak(O)^+$ in the denominator means its image $i(frak(O)^+)$.
entries.reason: The finite set S may be empty, in which case the natural homomorphism need not be injective. The quotient formula only requires its image.
entries.verified_by: The product decomposition in the proof of (49.40). For Λ=R=Z and A=Q, S is empty and O⁺={±1} maps to the trivial group. Replacing the asserted embedding by its natural image leaves the formula valid, including this case.

entries.corrected: Cl Λ ≅ Cl Λ₁ ⊕ Cl Λ₃

entries.verified_by: The preceding localized square and the following two descriptions of the first term.

entries.reason: The construction applies to the principal congruence subgroup W defined in the proof, not to every unit.
entries.verified_by: For n=6, d_i=3, the unit −1 has nontrivial image in the F₃ unit component, while B_(i+1) has trivial image there. The argument constructs the required image for the generators of W, and B_(i+1) is a factor of W.

entries.corrected: $G$ is trivial or has prime order.
entries.reason: The classification also includes the trivial group.
entries.verified_by: For G=1 the group ring is the maximal order ℤ and its kernel group is zero; Corollary (50.17) includes n=1.

entries.original: The powers $p^(n-1)$ and $2^(n-2)$ are used without separating the smallest groups.
entries.corrected: First set $e(1)=e(C_2)=1$; use the displayed bounds for the remaining groups.
entries.reason: Negative powers of a prime are not integer divisors of the exponent 1.
entries.verified_by: The kernel groups of the maximal order ℤ and of ℤC₂ are trivial. The positive-index proof and bounds are unchanged.

entries.reason: For q=1 the group is cyclic of order p.
entries.verified_by: The faithful cyclic complement has no nontrivial fixed point on C_p when q>1. The valid q=1 case of Theorem (50.25) is retained.

entries.place: Proof of (50.25), image in the unit-matrix paragraph
entries.reason: The displayed matrices are invertible, so the image being described is the image of the unit group.
entries.verified_by: Zero lies in the ring image but is not an invertible matrix; the following determinant square also has the unit group as domain.

entries.original: The two exact sequences are asserted for arbitrary $q divides p-1$ and $k>=0$.
entries.corrected: State them for even $q$ and $k>=1$, and put $G_0=H$.
entries.reason: For odd q an invariant p-primary summand can survive; the stated even-q regime has the two required exact sequences.
entries.verified_by: Hironaka (1979), Proposition 1.3 and its proof, specialize to D(ℤG_k)=D(ℤH)⊕(C_q′)^k⊕D(ℤC_(p^k))^H. For regular p and even q, inversion kills the invariant summand. Compatible quotient maps split off D(ℤH), and their remaining kernels are C_q′. The corresponding hereditary overorder and (49.25)(iii) give the class-group sequence. For p=7, q=3, k=2 the invariant weight-3 line instead supplies C₇.

entries.reason: The complement group contributes its own direct summand.
entries.verified_by: The split quotient G_k→H and the even-q specialization above retain D(ℤH). For p=17, q=16, k=1, (50.25) and (50.61) give C₈⊕C₂, not C₈.

entries.original: $D(ZZ G_k) tilde.equiv (C_(q'))^((k)) plus.o P$, with P a p-group.
entries.corrected: $D(ZZ G_k) tilde.equiv D(ZZ H) plus.o (C_(q'))^((k)) plus.o P$.
entries.reason: The p-primary term does not replace the direct summand from H.
entries.verified_by: Hironaka (1979), Proposition 1.3, gives P=D(ℤC_(p^k))^H in the single-Sylow specialization. The named historical result remains an attribution.

entries.place: General metacyclic paragraph, hypotheses and components
entries.original: Faithfulness is used to infer coprimality, and all cyclotomic components are treated as matrix algebras with maximal crossed orders.
entries.corrected: Assume $(n,q)=1$ and faithful action on every Sylow subgroup of C; separate the component ℚH for d=1, and use hereditary crossed orders for d>1.
entries.reason: Faithfulness on C alone gives neither coprimality nor faithful action on every component; the crossed orders need not be maximal.
entries.verified_by: Hironaka (1979), definition of D₀, Theorem 1.1, Proposition 1.3 and its proof. The action n=9,q=3,r=4 is faithful but not coprime. The action n=15,q=2,r=4 is not faithful on the C₃ component. The tame order ℤ[ζ₃]⋊C₂ has discriminant divisible by 3 and need not be maximal.

entries.place: General metacyclic paragraph, induction and order formula
entries.original: Induction is assigned target $D(ZZ G)$, and the displayed kernel-group order is inferred from the induction cokernel alone.
entries.corrected: Use target $D_0(ZZ G)=ker(D(ZZ G)->D(ZZ H))$ and write $abs(D(ZZ G))=abs(D(ZZ H)) abs(im f') (q')^(Omega(n))$.
entries.reason: The cokernel determines the quotient by the induction image, not the order of the entire kernel group.
entries.verified_by: Hironaka (1979), Proposition 1.3 and its proof, identify this induction target and cokernel. The split quotient to H gives the order formula. The original word “cokernel” is retained; the final arithmetic assertion is preserved only as the original attribution with its distinct map scope explained.

entries.place: Norm congruence in the proof of (50.31)
entries.reason: The needed congruence is the trace sum.
entries.verified_by: For α=a+bω, its trace is 2a+(2−π)b, which lies in πS₂. Taking α=ω disproves the printed difference congruence.

entries.reason: The displayed multiplicative group consists of the local units.
entries.verified_by: The residue field is F₂; the set excludes zero and every nonunit, and (50.33) already uses the unit group.

entries.reason: The norm-residue symbol is defined on the multiplicative group.
entries.verified_by: Zero is excluded by the norm interpretation and by the identities on the following page.

entries.place: Weber theorem, order of the primitive root
entries.reason: The real field in the stated signature count has degree $2^(n-1)$.
entries.verified_by: For n≥2 a primitive 2^n-th root instead gives real degree 2^(n−2). The corrected root order also gives ℚ when n=1.

entries.place: Trace form in the proof of (50.48)
entries.original: $T^+$ is the restriction of the regular trace form of A.
entries.corrected: $T^+$ is the intrinsic regular trace form of $A^+$.
entries.reason: The later value of the trace and its Gram matrix use multiplication on A⁺ itself.
entries.verified_by: For C₃ the two traces of 1 are 3 and 2. The difference of normalization is a p-adic unit factor in the argument, so the resulting p-parts are unchanged.

entries.original: Among the first 550 primes, 216 are irregular and 334 regular.
entries.corrected: Among the first 550 primes (2 through 3989), 218 are irregular and 332 regular, including 2 as regular for this count.
entries.reason: The finite numerical count is incorrect.
entries.verified_by: The exact Bernoulli numerators B₂ through B₃₉₈₆ agree in PARI and FLINT; divisibility for every odd prime in this range gives 218 irregular primes. The finite calculation is checks/sage/bernoulli.py; it does not prove the class-number criterion.

entries.place: Proof of (50.54), generator in Step 2 and final paragraph
entries.reason: Both subgroup occurrences must use the actual image 1−π.
entries.verified_by: For p=5 in F₅[π]/(π⁴), the linear coefficient would force (1+π)^4, whose quadratic coefficient is nonzero. The corrected generator still has leading degree 1, preserving the subsequent independence argument.

entries.place: Discussion following the Hilbert unit congruences
entries.original: Vanishing of δ(p) specified coefficients is taken to make δ(p) whole unit images equal 1.
entries.corrected: Only the specified leading coefficients vanish; these congruences no longer provide the same dimension bound.
entries.reason: Higher coefficients of arbitrary witnesses to the congruences need not vanish.
entries.verified_by: At p=37 one may choose the degree-34 unit also as the witness with a vanishing degree-32 leading coefficient. Its reduction modulo π³⁶ is still nontrivial. The theorem (50.56) and any more specifically normalized Hilbert construction are not thereby contradicted.

entries.place: Remark following (50.56), cyclic group of order p²
entries.corrected: A group of exponent dividing p.
entries.reason: The kernel group can be trivial.
entries.verified_by: For p=3, D(ℤC₉)=0, whose exponent is 1. The bound in (50.19) asserts divisibility.

entries.original: The formula uses f(s) with no definition of s and does not specify the discriminant convention.
entries.corrected: Put $s=m$ and interpret d as a discriminant ideal.
entries.reason: This gives the stated exponent f(m), and makes the factor ℤ in the displayed equality meaningful.
entries.verified_by: The different tower gives exponent (t+1)/2=f(m). Signed scalar discriminants would not satisfy the displayed ideal equality, already for ℚ(ζ₃).

entries.original: The Hint uses G/K as the crossed-order acting group and infers a faithful action from $K subset.eq ker chi$.
entries.corrected: Give the crossed-order argument when $J=ker chi$ is normal, with coefficient ring ℤ[η] for η of order |H/J| and complement G/H. Explain that the general conclusion remains the quoted result.
entries.reason: The original hypotheses do not make ker χ normal, and G/K has the wrong role in the crossed order.
entries.verified_by: For G=H=C₂,K=1 and nontrivial χ the printed rank is wrong. For G=A₄,H=V₄,K=1 a nontrivial χ has irreducible induction but nonnormal kernel. In the normal-kernel case Mackey’s criterion gives the faithful action on H/J, and the transversal supplies a unit-valued factor set to which Wilson’s theorem applies. These examples do not disprove the general conclusion.

entries.reason: The additive neighbourhood U is defined in (51.4).
entries.verified_by: The neighbourhood U is defined in (51.4); (51.2) defines a different additive neighbourhood.

entries.place: Example showing nondensity of principal idèles
entries.reason: The tuple must be an idèle, and the stated impossibility fails for x=±1.
entries.verified_by: A unit x makes the tuple an idèle. Valuations force m=0 for ±2^m x sufficiently close to 1, while x≠±1 makes the remaining finite set exclude 1.

entries.reason: The inverse difference must lie in the prescribed output neighbourhood.
entries.verified_by: The prescribed output neighbourhood is N. The input N′ was chosen so that the inverse difference lies in N, exactly as in (51.8).

entries.place: Definition of the normalized valuation after (51.8)
entries.original: smallest integer $m$ such that $a in P^m R_P$
entries.corrected: largest integer $m$ such that $a in P^m R_P$
entries.reason: The eligible exponents are all integers at most the valuation.
entries.verified_by: The eligible exponents form all integers at most the discrete valuation, since P^(m+1)R_P⊆P^mR_P. Their largest value defines the valuation.

entries.original: An arbitrary polynomial $g(x)$ is used without excluding zero endpoints; Exercise 2 assumes only irreducibility.
entries.corrected: First remove the factor $x^r$, require $g(0)!=0$, and plot nonzero-coefficient points. Exercise 2 also requires $g(0)!=0$.
entries.reason: Zero roots have infinite valuation and do not give finite sides of this Newton polygon.
entries.verified_by: Factor the polynomial as x^r g, with g(0) nonzero. Its nonzero roots have precisely the finite slopes in (51.12); a constant g has no finite sides. The exceptional irreducible polynomial is a scalar multiple of x.

entries.reason: Principal idèles need not equal 1 at almost all primes, as membership in $H^ast$ would require.
entries.verified_by: H is the closure of the principal subgroup u₀(A). A nonidentity principal unipotent norm-one matrix over ℚ need not be 1 at almost all primes, and thus need not belong to H*.

entries.reason: Endomorphisms of a left regular module use the opposite coefficient ring.
entries.verified_by: For left modules with ordinary composition, End_D(D^m)=M_m(D^op), consistently with (51.30). Passing to the opposite ring leaves the reduced-norm image unchanged.

entries.place: Coefficient expansion in the proof of (52.23)
entries.reason: The coefficient matrix requires summation over the output coset basis.
entries.verified_by: For H=1, G=C₂ and x=2+g, the inverse is (2−g)/3 and xg₁ has two nonzero basis coefficients.

entries.reason: The restricted element is evaluated by the H-character μ.
entries.verified_by: Formula (52.23) reads det_(μ^G)(x)=det_μ(res x). The restricted element lies in K₁(KH), where it is evaluated by the H-character μ.

entries.place: Membership sentence following the scalar comparison
entries.original: The right-hand expression is in $plus.minus H slash H'$.
entries.corrected: The underlying transfer class lies in $plus.minus H slash H'$.
entries.reason: The displayed character determinant is a scalar evaluation of that class.
entries.verified_by: The coset action is monomial. Its permutation sign and product of H-factors give the transfer class in ±H/H′; the character determinant then evaluates this class in E×.

entries.original: The induced restriction sends $[M]$ to $[N]+[R' G |_(R G)]$.
entries.corrected: The induced restriction sends $[M]$ to $[N]$; the stable class of the actual restricted lattice is $[M |_(R G)]=[N]+[R' G |_(R G)]$.
entries.reason: Reduced restriction and the class of the unreduced restricted lattice are different operations.
entries.verified_by: In K₀(RG), [Res M]=([N]−[RG])+[Res R′G]. Reduced restriction uses the common reference lattice Res R′G, whose local basis changes cancel. Its possibly nonzero Steinitz class remains in the separate unreduced-lattice formula.

entries.reason: The cited publication is the 1982 article, whose bibliography tag is corrected in C105.
entries.verified_by: Ullom’s cited article is from 1982. Its bibliography tag is corrected in C105; this is the separate occurrence of the same incorrect tag in Exercise 52.3.

entries.place: Nonzero representative in the Swan-module definition and Exercise 53.2
entries.original: The integer r is required only to be relatively prime to n.
entries.corrected: Take a nonzero integer r relatively prime to n.
entries.reason: The exceptional pair r=0,n=1 invalidates the later unit formulas and the injective map in the Hint.
entries.verified_by: Every unit residue modulo n has a nonzero representative prime to n, including n=1. No Swan class is lost. For r=0, the multiplication-by-r sequence in Exercise 2 is not injective and u/r is undefined.

entries.original: $overline(ZZ) tilde.equiv {plus.minus 1} times ("cyclic group of order" phi(n)/2)$

Then $c overline(R) subset.eq R$ and $overline(R) slash c overline(R)$ is finite. For the enveloping image $E$ and $Gamma=overline(R) E$, every lattice lies between $c Gamma I$ and $Gamma I$. Jordan–Zassenhaus and these finite quotients give finitely many bimodule classes without assuming tensor injectivity over $R$.

entries.original: The conjugate-containment equivalence is justified by Exercise 55.6.

entries.reason: Exercise 55.6 assumes a Dedekind domain, while the lemma permits an arbitrary integral domain.
entries.verified_by: Finite generation makes $T$ integral. Since $det T=1$, its inverse eigenvalues are integral too. A monic equation for $T^(-1)$, multiplied by a power of $T$, expresses the inverse in $R[T]$. Thus containment implies equality without restricting the lemma.

entries.place: Alternative proof of (74.11), final reduction argument
entries.original: Coefficient-field traces are used to infer absolute simplicity, and reduced multiplicity is used to infer Schur index one.
entries.corrected: Complete the proof using the center of the separable complete order, its unramified factors, lifted matrix units and a rank-one corner.
entries.reason: Simplicity of the reduction does not by itself imply absolute simplicity.
entries.verified_by: The two-dimensional simple module of $bb(F)_2 C_3$ is not absolutely simple. Averaging identifies the center after reduction. Its finite étale lift splits the complete order into factors whose reductions are full matrix algebras. Lift orthogonal primitive idempotents and matrix units. Each primitive corner is finite free of rank one over its central valuation ring; Nakayama gives that corner equal to the ring. Thus every factor is a full matrix algebra over an unramified extension, proving the original conclusion.

entries.place: Finite-prime presentation before the Hasse reciprocity formula
entries.original: $pi omega pi^(-1)=omega^(r_P)$ identifies a root exponent with the invariant numerator.
entries.corrected: Let $omega$ be a primitive $(q_P^(m_P)-1)$-st root. Choose $s_P$ with $r_P s_P≡1$ modulo $m_P$ and use arithmetic Frobenius to the power $s_P$, so $pi omega pi^(-1)=omega^(q_P^(s_P))$.
entries.reason: The exponent on a root is a power of the residue cardinality, not the numerator of the Hasse invariant.
entries.verified_by: For the cyclic algebra of arithmetic Frobenius and a prime element, fix invariant $1 slash m_P$. Replacing Frobenius by its $s_P$-th power replaces the numerator by its inverse modulo $m_P$, namely $r_P$. The Teichmüller root generates the unramified extension; $m_P=1$ is trivial. At index $3$ and residue cardinality $7$, root exponents $7$ and $49$ both reduce to $1$ modulo $3$ but correspond to different invariant numerators.

The assignments $n arrow psi(n)$ and $x_i arrow u_i$ respect the relations and surject onto the crossed product. The induced module maps isomorphically to its left regular module by $x_i times.o a arrow u_i a$; its character is $t psi_0$. A primitive idempotent has stabilizer $op("Gal")(K(omega) slash K)$, and its corner retains precisely the crossed-product basis indexed by that stabilizer. The restricted cocycle still has root-of-unity values. The conjugate idempotents sum to one, so the corner is full and represents the same Brauer class. This proves the corollary over every characteristic-zero field.

Conjugation and Möbius cancellation make its numerator divisible by $p$ unless there is a faithful action. A maximal faithfully acted-on subgroup has numerator $1$ modulo $p$, giving the full denominator. For the other branch $G=C_p times C_p$ gives $A(G)=p$; for the faithful branch $C_(91) ⋊ (C_3 times C_3)$ with separate faithful order-$3$ actions on $C_7$ and $C_(13)$ has coefficient $1 slash 9$.
